Index Funds Are Better When They’re Lucky and Smart
 
Plus, markets digest the blue tsunami
 

Markets are behaving a lot like they did the morning after President Trump’s surprise victory 10 years ago with stocks plunging overnight and then surging. Even parts of the market seen as more clearly tied to the losing side such as crypto seem to be getting over the shock based on premarket moves. There still are some obvious losers, such as the president’s eponymous media company and both Tesla and SpaceX, run by presidential buddy and Republican megadonor Elon Musk.

Turning off part of our brains

 

Back during the epic GameStop stock squeeze in 2021 that inspired the film “Dumb Money,” the headlines were all about YOLO traders supposedly making quick fortunes. 

 

A lot less attention was paid to professional investors who reaped bonanzas by just being in the right place at the right time. Quite a few cashed in, including Fidelity value maven Joel Tillinghast, “Big Short” legend Michael Burry and some lesser-known investors.

 

“It’s sort of like after the Super Bowl when they ask someone how it feels and they say it doesn’t feel real,” said one interviewed by The Wall Street Journal.

 

One you definitely didn’t hear about is the fuddiest, duddiest, most unlikely seller of a huge slug of GameStop shares after it rallied several thousand percent—Dimensional Fund Advisors. There’s a lesson in why that happened.

 

Dimensional is a mostly passive manager that says it goes “beyond indexing.” Its scientific approach attracts advisers and individuals who believe in academic ideas about factors such as value that drive long-run investing success.

 

Even so, why did a firm focused more on building a better mousetrap than stock picking dump a whopping $1 billion in GameStop for possibly its biggest single score ever? Because it incorporates common sense into its systematic approach.

 

“When indexing grew, it almost forced people to turn off a part of their brains,” says Joel Schneider, DFA’s deputy head of portfolio management.

 

Sometimes flying blind can be a good thing. For example, there are very few people who paid a split-adjusted one dollar for a share of Amazon and had the discipline to hang on by the time it had reached $250 a quarter-century later. Index funds stuck with Amazon through thick and thin.

 

Even smart (or lucky) professional active fund managers don’t do that. They can’t—professional risk and concentration rules force some selling once companies get huge.

 

As long as a stock continues to tick the boxes, indexes are too dumb to sell it. That, aside from low cost, is one of their advantages. The market’s long-run return is driven by a small number of massive winners that more than makes up for lots of duds. 

 

But what if the stocks in an index fund don’t resemble what’s on the label? In a very short span, GameStop and its fellow meme stock AMC Entertainment grew to dominate the Russell 2000 Value Index of small cap companies. They suddenly were neither small nor good value. GameStop was bigger than about half of the companies in the large cap S&P 500 index.

 

So DFA decided to cut and run. LSEG Russell, the owner of the widely followed small-cap benchmark, had to wait months to eject it, according to its rules. Much of the froth had come out of meme stocks by then.

 

The ethos of passive investing is taking the good with the bad. Intervening when it suits you seems to some almost like playing with nature, but Schneider points out that there’s nothing sacrosanct about popular benchmarks.

 

“There’s always human judgment—every index is a set of rules.”
